title: India Just Walked Away From a Quick Trade Deal With the U.S. The Bet Is That Washington Needs Delhi More.
excerpt: Buoyed by rising exports, a UK trade pact going live this month, and Goldman upgrading its growth forecast, India rejected an interim deal with Washington and is holding out for a tariff edge over China. The calculus matters for every Indian exporter and NRI-owned business on both sides.
body:
India has rejected a quick trade agreement with the United States in recent talks and is holding out for a substantially better deal, according to officials and analysts briefed on the negotiations — a striking turn from a country that, just months ago, was widely expected to be the first emerging market to ink a framework deal with the Trump administration.

After months of talks, New Delhi and Washington failed to finalise even an interim trade agreement during U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer's visit to New Delhi last month, despite expectations from both sides that a limited deal was within reach.

The breakdown came because Washington did not offer assurances on New Delhi's two non-negotiable demands: a tariff advantage over competitors such as China, and a guarantee that the U.S. would not impose new levies after the deal was signed.

"Our position is clear — we don't intend to rush into a deal that is not on favourable terms or compromise on red lines like ceding ground on agriculture," an Indian government official aware of the talks told Reuters.

## Why India Thinks It Can Wait

The confidence behind India's gambit is rooted in numbers that have shifted decisively in its favour over the past quarter.

In April–June 2026, India's overall goods exports rose about 15% from a year earlier despite disruptions from the Iran war, buoyed by pricier petroleum shipments. Exports to Gulf countries recovered to pre-war levels, climbing to $5.3 billion in May from $2.62 billion in March as traders routed shipments around the Strait of Hormuz. Exports to the United States edged up to $17.29 billion during April and May alone.

Goldman Sachs has raised its 2026 growth forecast for India to 6.8% and lowered its inflation and current-account deficit estimates — a combination that gives New Delhi more economic room to hold out for better terms. A weaker rupee has also improved exporters' competitiveness in dollar-denominated markets.

India is simultaneously broadening access to other developed markets. The India-UK Free Trade Agreement, or CETA, goes live on Tuesday, July 15 — the country's biggest trade deal in years. An EU agreement is expected by early next year.

"Indian negotiators have gained some leverage in the talks, given its strong economy, diversification initiatives with other partners, and its strategic standing in the world," said Wendy Cutler, senior vice president at the Washington-based Asia Society Policy Institute and a former U.S. trade official.

## Washington's Frustration

The United States had hoped for swift concessions from a strategic partner as President Trump prepares new tariffs likely to come into effect later this month, officials and analysts said. Like most countries, the bulk of Indian goods currently face a 10% U.S. tariff, but the administration is expected to introduce steeper levies through probes into excess industrial capacity. India denies U.S. charges of surplus capacity.

Washington has already proposed new tariffs of up to 12.5% on 54 economies, including India, over allegations they failed to curb trade in goods made with forced labour. India formally asked the USTR to reconsider this proposal in a July 6 submission, calling the evidentiary basis insufficient.

"The Trump administration continues to productively engage with Indian officials to finalise a historic trade deal that puts Americans and America First," White House spokesman Kush Desai said, responding to questions about the impasse.

A U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Washington remained engaged and still expected an agreement — but offered no timeline and noted that India had at times been "slow, bureaucratic and difficult" in the negotiations.

## The Waiting Game

India is also betting that some U.S. trade measures could face legal or political setbacks. A group of 22 Democratic state attorneys general have already filed objections to the Trump administration's proposed tariffs from the forced-labour probes. Legal uncertainty over U.S. tariffs, combined with Modi's recent state election victories, has helped India resist a rushed deal.

Indian Trade Minister Piyush Goyal said a day after talks with Greer that the U.S. deal "would not be implemented unless an advantage is ensured" — a statement analysts read as a clear signal that New Delhi sees no urgency. Indian Trade Secretary Rajesh Agrawal, the ministry's top official, echoed: "The framework deal is ready. Whenever it is the right time, it will be signed."

Senior leaders of the Bharatiya Janata Party have argued publicly that trade agreements should protect Indian farmers and small businesses — two politically influential constituencies that New Delhi has long shielded in trade negotiations.

"India realises that delaying — or even abandoning — a rushed deal may be more prudent than locking into obligations whose costs could far exceed any temporary tariff relief," said Ajay Srivastava, founder of the Global Trade Research Initiative and a former trade negotiator.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For the estimated 4.5 million Indian Americans and millions more NRIs with business ties across both countries, the impasse is anything but abstract. A tariff edge over China would benefit Indian IT services companies, pharmaceutical exporters, and the textile and manufacturing firms that employ hundreds of thousands of workers whose remittances flow back to families in India. Without a deal, the 12.5% forced-labour tariff and potential capacity-based levies could squeeze margins for small and mid-size Indian exporters who already operate on razor-thin profits.

The India-UK FTA going live this week offers some hedge — Indian professionals in Britain gain social security portability, and tariff reductions on textiles and engineering goods open a new corridor. But for diaspora businesses that straddle the India-U.S. corridor, the U.S. deal remains the one that matters most.

*Sources: Reuters, Asia Society Policy Institute, Goldman Sachs Research, India Ministry of Commerce*
